title: Yigdal
hookLine: Maimonides' thirteen principles put into verse

cards: Start with a dense page of philosophy: careful, argued, written in Arabic by a doctor and rabbi, Moses Maimonides, inside his commentary on the Mishnah. It lists thirteen things he says a Jew must hold to be true.
Now jump to a congregation on a Friday night, swaying, singing those same thirteen ideas to a bright melody.
Somewhere between the two, the list became a short Hebrew song, sung in many synagogues at the end of Friday night services. Philosophy, set to music.

teach.b: Yigdal means may he be magnified. It opens: magnified be the living God, and praised. The poem is usually credited to Daniel ben Judah, who lived in Rome in the fourteenth century.
He did something clever: he took Maimonides' thirteen principles and gave each one a line. God exists. God is one.
God has no body. God is first and last. Only God is to be worshipped.
The prophets spoke truly. Moses was the greatest of the prophets. The Torah was given from heaven.
It won't be exchanged. God knows our deeds. God rewards and punishes.
The redeemer will come. And the dead will live again, the hope the song ends on. Now the honest part.
Maimonides' list was never the only way to say what Judaism believes. Other thinkers argued with it.
Joseph Albo, in Spain, boiled the roots of faith down to three. Others asked whether faith can be a checklist at all, when so much of Judaism is about what you do.
Still, the list lasted, in songs like this one, and in a prose version, each line beginning I believe with perfect faith, printed in many prayer books after the morning service.

teach.h: A DEBATE A CHILD CAN SING.
teach.b: Yigdal turns a debate into something a child can sing.
In this tradition, ideas travel not only in books, but in the mouth.

how: Yigdal is printed at the start of the morning service in many prayer books and is often sung at the end of Friday night and festival evening services; a prose version of the thirteen principles, each beginning 'I believe with perfect faith', appears in many siddurim.

o: a bedtime prayer asking God for safe sleep
a psalm for the Sabbath sung by the Levites
may he be magnified: a song of thirteen beliefs

p: set them in verse, in Rome

s: every Jewish thinker accepted Maimonides' list of thirteen
others argued; Joseph Albo named three roots instead.
Yigdal has one line for each of the thirteen principles
Maimonides wrote the principles as a song
he wrote them in a commentary on the Mishnah; the song came later.

games.q: you're a Jewish poet in medieval Rome. you want a congregation to remember Maimonides' thirteen principles. what do you do?
o: read the commentary aloud each week.
give each principle one line of a song.
carve them over the synagogue door.
games.why: Daniel ben Judah, as tradition credits it, wrote thirteen lines, one per principle, and people still sing them.

practice: Don't reach for the biggest belief you have; find one that's true for you today, about God, or people, or how you want to live, or an honest doubt, and put it into one short sentence.
Say it out loud once, quietly, and hear how it sounds in the air instead of in your head.
